lines.text: This is the Cutting of the String, as Aun told it on the north cliff in his last winter, to whoever would hold the other end of a line.
Tell it slowly.
Count the knots as you go.
Among the lamps you will find the people who were in it: a child with a tailless kite, a gull, a boat with its lamp still lit.
I was the one with the knife.
I was a boy when Ennu gave me a tailless kite, cut from a sail too old to hold a boat.
It had two sticks and a bridle and no tail, so it spun and dropped and would not learn the wind.
I learned it on the cliff, fist by fist.
Then I wanted more than the wind's lesson.
I wanted to know its end.
Mother Hesk sat at the pole with her spindle, drawing the string thin and winding it on the whorl so the islands would not drift.
I came up the cliff with my knife in my belt, and she did not look round.
She said only, Mind the thread, Aun.
I said I would mind the wind.
Hesk wound every string the islands flew, and kept count of each knot in her two hands.
I cut at the pole, and the sky went up with a crack like a sail filling.
Hesk did not stop counting.
Her fingers went on knotting while the sky ran off.
I have never known whether that was cruelty or love, and I have had long winters to decide.
When I cut, Hesk's drop spindle slipped from her fingers in the wind and went over the edge of the pole.
The new thread, the one that would have held the sky close, went after it.
Somewhere below, I heard it strike the shingle.
Nobody has spun the sky since.
We have only the old string, and it is short.
I sent my word up to Vel, the Upper Sea, on a gull named Hilun, who carried messages between the islands and the sky.
She flew so close to the Gale that Tavo grew fond of her, and fond is a dangerous thing in a wind.
I asked her to tell the sky to come back.
She came down with Tavo's laugh in her feathers and no answer in her beak.
Sekra was the first gull to follow me up the cut string.
She wanted to see where the wind went too, and I did not send her back.
She flew so high that frost stiffened her wings.
I watched her go white against the blue, still climbing, and I did not call her down.
I was glad of company.
I am not glad now.
I cut it because I wanted to know how far the wind went.
That was the whole reason, and it was a poor one.
The sky drifted off with me holding the knife, and every kite I had flown on that string went with it.
My hands still remember the line.
For a long time I was proud of the question.
I did not cut it clean.
The Sun-Kite was still tied to my wrist, so it went up with the others, and its ribbon came loose and streamed away across the Lamp Road.
Ennu had sewn that kite to carry the sun through the year.
Now the people of the islands reckon the year by a ribbon they cannot reach, and I am the one who tied it on.
Sil ran after the sky along the tide, my sister, the Moon, with her skirts in the wrack and her voice going up the wind.
Before I could let go, I had tied a stone to the last line, as if a stone could keep a sky.
I still feel the weight in my palm.
She is searching still.
Each night she comes up low over the water, looking for a brother who will not be found.
Tirun came home keel-up on a grey morning, with no crew in her and no oars shipped.
The women of the north shore turned her with ropes and found her lamps still lit underneath.
They asked me why the sky had no lamp for her.
I had no answer.
Nobody had counted her: not the sea, not the Reel, not me.
When a child goes into the sea, the mother climbs to the cliff on the first still day, when the wind has finally let go of the water.
She ties a small kite and flies it over the rocks, so the child has something to look for.
I have watched a hundred mothers do it.
I have no child to fly one for.
I had only a string, and I chose to cut it.
Ennu sat on the cliff with a bone needle and a bolt of sailcloth, making a gull for a woman whose husband had gone out and not come back.
I held the cloth taut for him.
He asked me to hold it straight.
I did not.
I was thinking of the sky, and the seam went crooked, and that gull still flies with a list to one side.
The first things past the last lamp were the drowned, and none of them knew the way.
A boatman of the Upper Sea, grey-bearded, took them across for nothing, because the crossing is unpaid.
I went down to the water and asked for passage.
He told me I had not drowned, so I had no fare.
He was not unkind.
He was counting, as Hesk counts, and I was not on his list.
The sky went up but did not come all the way free.
A short length of cord stayed knotted to my hand, and it still hangs at the bottom of the Unflown, where the wind does not come back.
I hold the other end.
Each night I tell the sky what I did, and each night it does not answer.
Fly back, I say.
I am still holding the knife.
